text:
Code
# Force UTF-8 so unicode (mL/min/1.73m², ±, ≥) renders correctly.
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_ALL", "en_US.UTF-8"))

# Lightweight install guard so the project renders on a fresh machine.
.need <- c("readxl","dplyr","tidyr","purrr","tibble","flextable","officer","ggplot2","rvg")
.miss <- setdiff(.need, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(.miss)) install.packages(.miss, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
# bodycompref is GitHub-only (p-mq/bodycompref); supplies the muscle Z-score.
if (!requireNamespace("bodycompref", quietly = TRUE)) {
  if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("remotes", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  remotes::install_github("p-mq/bodycompref")
}

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(flextable)
library(ggplot2)

# Output directory for downloadable Word copies of every table.
docx_dir <- "docs/tables/heatmap"
dir.create(docx_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# Absolute path: flextable_to_rmd() can change the working directory mid-render,
# which would break later saves to a relative docx_dir.
docx_dir <- normalizePath(docx_dir, mustWork = TRUE)

save_ft_docx <- function(ft, name) {
  flextable::save_as_docx(ft, path = file.path(docx_dir, paste0(name, ".docx")))
  invisible(ft)
}

# Output directory for downloadable PowerPoint copies of the plot panels.
ppt_dir <- "docs/ppt"
dir.create(ppt_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# Absolute path for the same reason as docx_dir (cwd can change mid-render).
ppt_dir <- normalizePath(ppt_dir, mustWork = TRUE)

# Render a list of ggplots inline AND write them to an editable .pptx (one slide
# per plot) under docs/ppt/, then print a Markdown download link. Must be called
# inside a `results: asis` chunk. Editable vector via rvg::dml; raster fallback.
emit_plots <- function(plots, fname,
                       label = "⬇️ Download these panels as PowerPoint (editable)") {
  for (p in plots) print(p)                                   # figures, inline
  loc <- officer::ph_location(left = 0.5, top = 1.2, width = 9, height = 5.14)  # 7:4
  doc <- officer::read_pptx()
  for (p in plots) {
    doc <- officer::add_slide(doc, layout = "Title and Content", master = "Office Theme")
    gr  <- tryCatch(rvg::dml(ggobj = p), error = function(e) NULL)
    doc <- officer::ph_with(doc, if (is.null(gr)) p else gr, location = loc)
  }
  print(doc, target = file.path(ppt_dir, paste0(fname, ".pptx")))
  cat(sprintf("\n\n[%s](../ppt/%s.pptx)\n\n", label, fname))
}

# --- Two colouring schemes -------------------------------------------------
# V1: 4-level categorical severity.  <5 yellow · 5–10 orange · 10–20 red · >20 purple.
cat4_fill <- function(x) {
  dplyr::case_when(is.na(x) ~ "#FFFFFF",
                   x <  5  ~ "#FFEDA0",   # yellow
                   x < 10  ~ "#FEB24C",   # orange
                   x <= 20 ~ "#F03B20",   # red
                   TRUE    ~ "#6A51A3")   # purple
}

# V2: continuous gradient across `stops` (low 0 % -> high), saturating at `dom` %.
# (base grDevices, no extra dependency). The exact % is printed in every cell.
ramp_fill <- function(x, stops, dom = 30) {
  f   <- grDevices::colorRamp(stops)
  x2  <- pmin(pmax(x, 0), dom) / dom
  out <- rep("#FFFFFF", length(x))      # NA -> white (no data)
  ok  <- !is.na(x2)
  if (any(ok)) {
    m <- f(x2[ok])
    out[ok] <- grDevices::rgb(m[, 1], m[, 2], m[, 3], maxColorValue = 255)
  }
  out
}
# Yellow -> orange -> red ramp for Part B (low % = yellow, high % = deep red).
CONT_STOPS <- c("#FFEDA0", "#FEB24C", "#F03B20", "#B2182B")

title: Chemotherapy Dosing: eGFR Equations vs Measured GFR (OncoGFR 1200)
text:
Muscle Z-score (LOESS, 465 body-composition cohort)
Y = % over- (or under-) dosed; x = muscle Z-score (SMI). Mechanistically, lower muscle Z (less muscle) lowers serum creatinine, so creatinine-based equations can read GFR falsely high → overdose; cystatin-based equations are muscle-independent. The curves show how this plays out across the muscle spectrum (CIs widen at the sparse extremes). N = 465; indexed GFR.
Z-score provenance. The Z is computed in this document with the bodycompref package (v2.0.1) — reference_z_scores(metric = "SMI", level = "L3", …), a GAMLSS LMSP model fit to Framingham Heart Study CT data (Tonnesen et al., Invest Radiol 2023) — rather than the stored z_score column, which came from an older build with an age floor of 35. ⚠️ Reference window is age 38–80, but this cohort spans 19–86, so 58 / 465 (12.5 %) patients (46 younger than 38, 12 older than 80) are clamped to a boundary age and their Z is anchored to an age they are not — read the extremes of the muscle spectrum with that in mind.

title: Chemotherapy Dosing: eGFR Equations vs Measured GFR (OncoGFR 1200)
text:
Derived dose variables
Per-patient binary flags (1 = yes, 0 = no), computed for each equation on the indexed scale vs measured GFR (whole 1,200 cohort):







Variable
Definition (per equation, vs mGFR)




cisplatin_eligible
equation GFR ≥ 40 → cisplatin-eligible (not “avoid”)


carbo15_over
Calvert dose > 15 % above the mGFR AUC-5 dose


carbo15_under
Calvert dose > 15 % below the mGFR AUC-5 dose


carbo20_over
Calvert dose > 20 % above the mGFR AUC-5 dose


carbo20_under
Calvert dose > 20 % below the mGFR AUC-5 dose



The code that creates them (click ▸ Code to expand):


Code
dose_vars <- purrr::map_dfr(reg$equation, function(eq) {
  g <- dat[[reg$index_col[reg$equation == eq]]]   # this equation's indexed GFR
  m <- dat$mGFRindex                              # measured GFR (indexed)
  tibble::tibble(
    equation = eq, ecog_grp = dat$ecog_grp,
    cisplatin_eligible = as.integer(dose_tier(g, "cisplatin") > 0),
    carbo15_over  = as.integer(carbo_class(g, m, 5.75, 4.25) == "Overdose"),
    carbo15_under = as.integer(carbo_class(g, m, 5.75, 4.25) == "Underdose"),
    carbo20_over  = as.integer(carbo_class(g, m, 6, 4)       == "Overdose"),
    carbo20_under = as.integer(carbo_class(g, m, 6, 4)       == "Underdose"))
}) %>% dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(reg, equation, type, label), by = "equation")


Overall rate (% yes) of each flag, by equation:


Code
dose_vars %>%
  dplyr::transmute(Equation = paste(type, "·", label),
                   cisplatin_eligible, carbo15_over, carbo15_under, carbo20_over, carbo20_under) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Equation) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), ~ round(mean(.x) * 100, 1)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Equation", "Cispl. eligible %", "Carbo15 over %",
                             "Carbo15 under %", "Carbo20 over %", "Carbo20 under %"))

title: Chemotherapy Dosing: eGFR Equations vs Measured GFR (OncoGFR 1200)
text:
Sensitivity 1 — absolute eGFR difference (Cys − Cr)
CKD-EPI Cys 2012 − CKD-EPI Cr 2021, in mL/min/1.73 m² — the same discordance left unscaled instead of divided by the creatinine estimate. Unlike the percentage version this one is not scale-invariant, so it is taken on the indexed scale, the conventional way to read a difference between two equations. The dashed marker is at 0 (the two equations agree); the −10 % marker of the other panels is a percentage and has no counterpart here.

  overlay_plot(cl_nonindex, eq, xvar = "egfr_diff", xlab = DIFF_XLAB, xlim = DIFF_XLIM,
               binw = 5, pct_axis = FALSE, ref_at = 0,
               xscale = tick_x(DIFF_BREAKS, pct = FALSE))),
  "carbo20-sens-absdiff")

title: Chemotherapy Dosing: eGFR Equations vs Measured GFR (OncoGFR 1200)
Chemotherapy Dosing: eGFR Equations vs Measured GFR (OncoGFR 1200)
OncoGFR 1200 — Chemotherapy Dosing by eGFR Equation
text:
A sub-analysis of the dose project using the OncoGFR 1200 cohort, which uniquely includes a measured GFR (mGFR, ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance) as the gold standard.
The analysis asks: if chemotherapy were dosed from each estimated-GFR (eGFR) equation instead of measured GFR, how often would patients be over- or under-dosed? Every comparison is run on both the indexed (mL/min/1.73 m²) and non-indexed (absolute mL/min) GFR scale, with measured GFR as the reference throughout.
Two views of that question:

Dosing Heatmaps — the full exploratory grid: every equation × drug × subgroup, as heatmaps, plus LOESS sets against several kidney-function contrasts, the carboplatin ±20 % panels (with three definitions of eGFR difference), the manuscript heatmaps, and Table 1 for the Fried frailty cohort.
Grant figures — a focused cut for the grant: carboplatin only, plotted against the eGFRcr-cys / Cockcroft-Gault discordance index, with the cohort distribution and an overdose-threshold breakdown by frailty and cachexia. This page now lives on the separate Grant site, alongside the Sherley carboplatin figures that use the same index.
Dosing Heatmaps →
Grant figures → — carboplatin overdose risk vs the eGFRcr-cys / Cockcroft-Gault discordance index. Moved to the separate Grant site on 2026-09-29; the codebook below still documents it.



Cockcroft-Gault · CKD-EPI Cr (2021) · CKD-EPI Cys · CKD-EPI Cr-Cys (2021) · EKFC Cr · EKFC Cys · EKFC Cr-Cys · CKD-EPI 4-marker



Exploratory sections — Carboplatin (Calvert AUC 5) · Cisplatin · Methotrexate · Melphalan.
Final heatmaps (the manuscript tables) — the same carboplatin and cisplatin plus the seven drugs of final_chemos.docx: Pemetrexed · Etoposide · Capecitabine · Bleomycin · Ifosfamide · Melphalan · Methotrexate. Those thresholds supersede the earlier rules; carboplatin and cisplatin are not in that document and keep their existing rules.
Carboplatin overdose is defined against a tolerance band: ±15 % and ±20 % on the Dosing Heatmaps page, and ≥10 %, ≥15 % and ≥20 % on the Grant page.

C. Concepts
C1 · Measured GFR is the gold standard. Every “overdose” on this page is defined against ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance, not against another estimate. So the figures measure estimation error with a clinical consequence, not disagreement between two guesses.
C2 · Indexed vs absolute GFR. Indexed GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) rescales everyone to a standard body size — right for staging CKD, because it makes patients comparable. Absolute GFR (mL/min) is the patient’s actual clearance — right for dosing, because a drug is cleared by the kidney the patient actually has. The relationship is absolute = indexed × BSA / 1.73 (verified in this dataset). Using an indexed GFR in Calvert systematically misdoses anyone whose body size is far from average, which is why the absolute scale is the primary analysis here.
C3 · Calvert and where the constants come from. Carboplatin is dosed to a target exposure: dose = AUC × (GFR + 25). At AUC 5 the dose is 5(GFR + 25). Overdosing by more than a fraction t means
\[5(\text{eGFR}+25) > (1+t)\cdot 5(\text{mGFR}+25)\]
so the right-hand constant is 5(1+t): 5.5 at 10 %, 5.75 at 15 %, 6 at 20 %. The mirror-image constants 5(1−t) give underdose. That is the whole of carbo_class() and carbo_over_thr() — the apparently magic 6 and 4 are just ±20 %.
C4 · The discordance index. (eGFRcr-cys − Cockcroft-Gault) / Cockcroft-Gault × 100. Cystatin C is not raised by muscle mass, so in a wasted patient creatinine stays deceptively low and Cockcroft-Gault reads high, while cystatin pulls the combined equation down. A negative index therefore flags “Cockcroft-Gault is flattering this kidney”. Because it is a ratio of two GFRs on the same scale, the BSA factor cancels — indexed and absolute versions agree to within 0.5 points here (rounding only).
C5 · Why the index is more discriminating for some equations. Cockcroft-Gault is the index’s own denominator, so the CG panel is partly self-referential and shows the steepest gradient (78.5 % → 1.2 %). The CKD-EPI Cr 2021 panel is a genuinely independent test and is much flatter (33 % → 15 %). Both are shown; only the second is independent evidence.
C6 · LOESS and the clipping. The outcome is binary per patient (overdosed or not). LOESS takes a locally weighted average of those 0/1 values in a sliding window (span = 0.9), which estimates the probability of overdose as a smooth function of the index. It is unconstrained, so where data are sparse it can return values above 100 % or below 0 % — the raw Cockcroft-Gault fit reached ~105 %. The drawn curve and band are therefore clipped to [0, 100]. The fit is not modified, so a curve lying flat on 0 % at the far right is at the edge of the data, not a genuine plateau.
C7 · The dual axis in Figure 3. Two quantities with different units share one panel. The overdose curve owns the left axis (0–100 %). The bars are drawn as count / CNT_MAX × 100 so they occupy the same 0–100 range, and the right axis inverts exactly that transform to relabel them as counts (or as % of cohort). Bar heights are identical in both variants — only the right-hand labelling changes. The right axis and the bars share a colour so the mapping needs no legend.
C8 · Exact binomial CIs. Figure 4’s smallest cell is 113 patients (Frail) with ~10 events. Normal-approximation intervals are unreliable that sparse and can run below zero, so the Clopper-Pearson exact interval is used instead. Overlapping intervals across groups are the reason the frailty and cachexia contrasts are reported as null.
C10 · Recovering an undocumented coding. Neither the frailty nor the nutrition file ships a codebook, so what 0/1/2 and 1/2 mean had to be recovered rather than assumed. The method is to predict what each candidate mapping implies for other variables and check which holds. Frailty should track age and performance status — it does, monotonically, so 0 = non-frail through 2 = frail. Nutrition rating should track cachexia — and there the answer inverts the intuitive reading: rating 1 is the malnourished group. This matters beyond labelling, because ASG-PPP is the only marker in Figure 4 with a visible separation, and knowing its direction turns an apparent confirmation of the grant hypothesis into a contradiction of it.
C9 · Why the −10 % line. A single fixed reference at −10 % replaces the old zero line and cohort-median line. Zero is not the clinically interesting point — it is where two estimates agree, which says nothing about dosing. −10 % sits where the overdose curve begins to climb steeply, so it reads as a candidate flag threshold rather than a statistical artefact.
